subsystems.name: Cell source and expansion
subsystems.role: provides the patient's own skin cells so the graft is not rejected.

subsystems.name: Bioink
subsystems.role: a printable carrier that holds cells in place and later becomes the matrix.
parts: hydrogel precursors (collagen, fibrin, alginate, hyaluronic acid)

subsystems.name: Bioprinter
subsystems.role: deposits the layers in a defined pattern onto a surface or directly into a wound.

subsystems.name: Dermal scaffold
subsystems.role: gives the graft mechanical strength and a template for blood vessels to grow into.

subsystems.name: Maturation system
subsystems.role: grows the printed construct into a layered tissue before grafting.

subsystems.name: Release testing
subsystems.role: proves the graft is sterile, viable and genetically normal before it touches a patient.

buildSteps.title: Take a biopsy
buildSteps.detail: About 1–2 cm² of the patient's own skin is taken from an uninjured site and transported to a clean lab.

buildSteps.title: Separate the cell types
buildSteps.detail: Enzymes break the tissue down; keratinocytes and fibroblasts are isolated and grown in separate cultures.

buildSteps.title: Expand the cells
buildSteps.detail: Over roughly 2–4 weeks the cells multiply to tens of millions, enough to seed a graft covering a much larger area than the biopsy.

buildSteps.title: Formulate the bioink
buildSteps.detail: Cells are mixed into a hydrogel whose viscosity and stiffness suit the printer and the target layer — fibroblasts for the deep layer, keratinocytes for the surface.

buildSteps.title: Print the layers
buildSteps.detail: The printer builds the construct layer by layer in a sterile enclosure, placing dermal cells in the base and surface cells on top, shaped to the wound.

buildSteps.title: Stabilise and mature
buildSteps.detail: The printed gel is crosslinked so it holds shape, then kept in a bioreactor; lifting it to an air–liquid interface makes the surface cells flatten and keratinise.

buildSteps.title: Test and package
buildSteps.detail: Samples are checked for sterility, viability and normal chromosomes, and the graft is packed for surgery within a short window.

buildSteps.title: Graft and dress
buildSteps.detail: Surgeons place the sheet on the prepared wound bed, secure it and cover it so the graft can take and the vessels can grow in.

prerequisites.why: cultured epidermal autografts for burns have been used clinically since the 1980s, so cell expansion itself is proven.
laser-assisted and extrusion bioprinting of skin cells has been demonstrated for grafts and for lab testing, but not yet at routine clinical scale.
grafts thicker than about a millimetre starve for oxygen unless blood vessels reach them quickly; printing pre-formed vessels is unsolved.
hair follicles, sweat and oil glands are not reproduced, so the graft is functional skin but not complete skin.

prerequisites.tech: Regulatory route for living cell products
prerequisites.why: living-cell therapies need bespoke safety and manufacturing rules, and the pathway is still developing in most countries.

pathway.milestone: autologous cell sprays and cultured epidermal sheets are used to close burns, alongside acellular and donor-cell skin substitutes
pathway.unlocks: routine wound cover where a patient's own cells are available.

pathway.milestone: bioprinted bilayered autologous grafts reach late-stage clinical trials for burns and scars
pathway.unlocks: a defined, reproducible replacement that includes both the dermal and surface layers.

pathway.milestone: printing directly into the wound during surgery
pathway.unlocks: coverage of irregular burns in one procedure rather than weeks of lab culture.

pathway.milestone: vascularised grafts carrying follicles and glands
pathway.unlocks: skin that restores sweating, sensation and hair, useful for chronic wounds and reconstruction, not only burns.
